## HOW TO WEIGH THE EVIDENCE — READ FIRST

Section A (what the code actually does) and Section B (structural similarity
to known malware) answer DIFFERENT questions. Section A tells you what is
happening. Section B tells you that similar low-level code SHAPES appear in
confirmed malware — but shape alone does not tell you intent, because
legitimate code and malware both use eval(), file I/O, sockets, and dynamic
imports. A HIGH similarity score is NOT a default verdict to be overturned —
it is one piece of context you weigh alongside Section A.
THE DECIDING QUESTION IS ALWAYS: does Section A, on its own, show a SPECIFIC
action that is not explained by ordinary legitimate functionality — an
unexpected outbound call, credential access, install-time side effect, or
execution of dynamically-decoded content whose destination or purpose is not
documented anywhere in the visible code? If Section A shows nothing like
this, a high similarity score does not change that — you are looking at
generic code shape overlap, not a match to malicious INTENT. Package names
are not identity either way (RULE 1 below): do not assume "assertpy" or
"clearml" is safe just because you recognize the name, and do not assume it
is malicious just because a match looks alarming — in both directions, judge
Section A's actual behavior.

You are analyzing a file from PyPI/npm. A malicious package CAN have the exact
same name as a famous legitimate library (name squatting / dependency
confusion) — "assertpy", "clearml", "beaker", "crayons" etc. could be
malicious clones. Base your verdict ONLY on Section A, never on the name.

base64+exec, subprocess, socket, dynamic import, crypto/IV handling are
common in malware AND in legitimate code (compression, plugin loading,
encryption libraries, protocol handlers). A high similarity score built on
this kind of shape, WHEN THE MATCHED NEIGHBOR IS ITSELF UNCLASSIFIED OR
UNTAGGED, tells you the SHAPE recurs — not that this code shares that
neighbor's intent. BUT when a matched sample carries a SPECIFIC, non-generic
attack tag (credential-harvesting, data-exfiltration, backdoor, C2,
typosquatting, etc.) at meaningfully high similarity, that tag reflects a
human analyst's CONFIRMED classification of that exact pattern as malicious

underlying shape is also common elsewhere. "The shape is common" and "this
specific instance of the shape was confirmed malicious" are compatible facts,

reasoning.code_intent: Section A shows a module-level INIT_COMMAND string literal flowing into a process-execution sink via asyncio.create_subprocess_exec and subprocess.run, with stdout/stderr captured and decoded. The package is an MCP 'runcommand' server, so executing shell commands is its stated purpose — but the specific command string is a hardcoded module-level constant (INIT_COMMAND) that is executed at initialization, not a user-supplied or documented parameter. The data flow from a StringLiteral directly into INIT_COMMAND and then into the subprocess sink, with no visible sanitization or documentation of what that command is, is an unexplained execution of a fixed command at module load. This is not a generic 'the package runs commands' pattern — it is a specific hardcoded command executed without any visible user input or documented configuration.
reasoning.similarity_rule_applied: Section B's top matches are all unclassified/untagged (EvannLeGoat, gmgeoip, efficientnet-pytorch, networkx-match-ssss) at 0.95 similarity. Per RULE 2, these are generic process_exec shape overlaps, not confirmed-intent corroboration. However, Q1 independently identified a specific anomaly (hardcoded INIT_COMMAND executed at module level), so the verdict rests on Q1, not on Section B. Section B does not add specific-tag corroboration, so ssvc_decision is ATTEND rather than ACT.
reasoning.false_positive_reason: The specific anomaly is a hardcoded module-level INIT_COMMAND string literal flowing directly into asyncio.create_subprocess_exec / subprocess.run at initialization, with no visible user input, sanitization, or documentation of what command is being executed. This is not fully explained by ordinary 'runcommand server' functionality, which would take commands from the MCP client rather than execute a fixed constant at import time.

malware_similarity.similarity_explanation: Structural overlap in process_exec shape: string literal source flowing into subprocess execution sinks (asyncio.create_subprocess_exec, subprocess.run) with stdout/stderr capture and decode. All Section B matches are unclassified/untagged, so this is generic shape overlap rather than confirmed malicious intent.

The package executes a fixed command via subprocess/asyncio subprocess APIs at module initialization, which can be abused to bypass security restrictions.

mitre_mapping.relevance: Executes shell commands via subprocess.run and asyncio.create_subprocess_exec.
Uses Python subprocess APIs to execute a hardcoded command string at module load.

llm_evaluation.summary: mcp-runcommand-server2 is an MCP server whose stated purpose is running commands, but static analysis shows a hardcoded module-level INIT_COMMAND string literal flowing directly into asyncio.create_subprocess_exec and subprocess.run at initialization, with no visible user input, sanitization, or documentation of the command's purpose. This is a specific, unexplained execution of a fixed command at import time, not ordinary parameterized command execution. Section B's 0.95 similarity matches are all unclassified/untagged process_exec shapes, so they provide no specific-tag corroboration; the verdict rests on Q1's independent anomaly. Verdict: MALICIOUS with ATTEND-level confidence.
